lines.speaker: A
lines.text: You loved a movie and want more like it. How does a computer know which ones feel alike? Antoine taught this as a three-part story, and it starts with turning movies into numbers.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Numbers? How do you turn a movie into numbers?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: With embeddings. He combines a movie's title, year, genres, cast, director and summary into text, and an encoder turns it into a list of numbers, a vector. Similar movies end up close together. Think of a map where movies about the same thing cluster like neighbourhoods.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And Part 1 is where that lives?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, in PostgreSQL with pgvector. The vectors sit beside the normal columns, and finding nearest neighbors becomes plain SQL: order by distance, limit ten. Antoine compared five models, BART, GTE, MiniLM, RoBERTa and e5-large, and also cosine and Euclidean distance. Cosine compares the angle between vectors, so a short and a long text about the same topic still match.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It moves to Qdrant with MovieLens, behind a FastAPI app. There are two kinds of vectors. Dense ones, 384 numbers, encode the title and genres, to answer titles that read like this query. Sparse ones encode each user's ratings, to answer users with similar taste.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Your ratings become a sparse query. Qdrant finds the twenty nearest users, and the app adds up their ratings for movies you haven't seen. The top five are your recommendations. It's like asking twenty people with your taste what they loved. The web app lets you pick the dataset, either MovieLens one hundred K or one million, and a mode, by ratings or by title and genre.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Retrieval plus a local language model. The pgvector rows become evidence. The question is embedded, a nearest-neighbors query pulls the top movies, and a prompt gives those rows to an Ollama model through LangChain, so the answer is grounded in the same catalog.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly: plot language, taste overlap, and explaining why. The notebooks and animations are in the AlgoETS repository, and the write-up has the diagrams.
